sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Magni** (*magni*) — Strength, Son of Thor · The Strong One — is the prodigy of the Norse corpus: the son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa who, at three nights old, freed his father from under the fallen Hrungnir's leg when all the Æsir together could not move it.[^1]

Old Norse *Magni* is the common noun *magn*/*megn* 'strength, might' made personal: 'the strong one'. The sources know him in two scenes and a promise — the lifting at Grjótúnagarðar, the gift of the gold-maned horse Gullfaxi that Óðinn reproved, and the prophecy of *Vafþrúðnismál* that after Ragnarǫk Magni and his brother Móði shall have Mjǫllnir, the hammer of their fallen father.[^1][^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Magni** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography and never about the god. The temple is domain-less: the plain-ASCII *magni.com* is held by a third party outside the collection and watched for release; no form of the name is owned, and this temple claims none.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17 (the Hrungnir duel; Magni lifts the leg), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Vafþrúðnismál 51; Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 53, trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014), and Faulkes (1987).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Magni, magn.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Magni** (nominative; genitive *Magna*, as in Hárbarðsljóð 53: *Magna faðir*, 'Magni's father'). It is a transparent formation on the Old Norse common noun *magn*/*megn* 'strength, might, main' — hence 'the strong one' — from Proto-Germanic *maginą 'strength, power'.[^1] The same root gives Old English *mægen* 'strength, force' (surviving in the phrase 'with might and main') and stands beside the verb *magan* 'be able', the ancestor of English *may* and *might*.[^2]

Unlike Þórr or Baldr, the name ends in *-i*: it is a weak ja-stem formation, so it carries no nominative *-r*. The ASCII fallback *magni* therefore loses nothing at all — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no ending — and the mechanical tier rule places the name in Tier 2 on a purely orthographic report.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

No domain is held for this name. Because *Magni* is pure ASCII, *magni.com* was registered long ago in the ordinary way and is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection; the project watches it for release, and this temple claims no address it does not own.[^3]

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. magn, Magni.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Magni, magn.
Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Magni.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈmɑɣ.ni/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ma-** — Voiced bilabial nasal [m] and short open back [ɑ]; stress falls on the first syllable, as in every Old Norse word
- **-gni** — The medial g is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ], softer than the English stop; then dental nasal [n] and short close [i]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'MAHG-ni' — a short open 'ah', the g softened between the vowels. Modern Icelandic, where the name is still living, hardens the g to [k]: 'MAHK-ni'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Magni, 'the strong one', son of Þórr and Járnsaxa
- **Younger Futhark** — ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i); the ᚴ rune writes g, and there is no nominative -r to carve
- **Proto-Germanic** — *maginą, 'strength, power'
- **Modern Icelandic** — Magni, unchanged in spelling for a thousand years[^2]

Magni is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no lost ending. The strongest boy in the Edda has one of its plainest names.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Magni.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Magni** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and of the Prose Edda, recording material centuries older.[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the younger futhark; the god's name is not attested in runes, but as a human name Magni does occur in the inscriptional record, so the runic rendering is more than a theoretical exercise.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a ja-stem formation on *magn*/*megn* 'strength', ending in *-i*; there is no nominative *-r* as in Þórr or Baldr.
- Old Norse orthography writes no diacritic in this name: five plain Latin letters.
- In the Younger Futhark the name runs ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i); the ᚴ rune writes both k and g, and the short a and i need no qualification.
- The ASCII form *magni* therefore loses nothing — the restoration differs from the input only by the capital, which is why the mechanical rule places the name in Tier 2.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Magni; Peterson, Lena, Nordiskt runnamnslexikon, 5th ed. (2007), s.v. Magni.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Magni** is catalogued under Strength, Son of Thor — and both halves of the domain are simply the content of his myth.[^1]

### Strength

His name is the common noun for strength itself, and his one feat is pure strength: lifting Hrungnir's stone leg off his father when the assembled Æsir could not.

### Son of Þórr

Skáldskaparmál's kennings for Þórr begin with his fatherhood — 'father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr' — and Hárbarðsljóð closes Þórr's self-naming with the same fact: *Magna faðir*.

### The Inheritance

Vafþrúðnismál 51 and Gylfaginning 53 agree: after Ragnarǫk, Magni and his brother Móði shall have Mjǫllnir — the hammer passing whole from the fallen father into the renewed world.[^2]

### Youth

He does it all at three nights old: the Edda's only divine childhood, and the proof the tradition offers that strength answers to nature, not to age.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17 (the lifting) and kennings for Þórr ('father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr'), trans. Faulkes (1987); Hárbarðsljóð 53, trans. Larrington (2014).
Vafþrúðnismál 51, trans. Larrington (2014); Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 53, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
Magni's iconography is narrative rather than cultic — the corpus gives him no temple and no regalia of his own, but his two scenes fixed a small set of attributes:[^1]

- **Hrungnir's leg** — The stone giant's fallen limb across Þórr's neck: the weight no god could move, and the boy's single feat
- **Gullfaxi** — 'Gold-mane', Hrungnir's stallion, given to Magni as the prize of the lifting — the gift that drew Óðinn's reproof: so fine a horse should not go to a giantess's son
- **Mjǫllnir** — Not yet his: the hammer he inherits with Móði after Ragnarǫk, the one treasure of the old world promised to the new[^2]
- **The whetstone shard** — The fragment of Hrungnir's weapon lodged in Þórr's head at the same duel: the scar that remained when the leg was lifted
- **Móði** — 'Wrath', his brother, named with him in both inheritance passages: the Edda never lets the heirs be counted singly[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Vafþrúðnismál 51; Gylfaginning 53; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Magni, Móði.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Magni's mythology is two scenes and a promise, told across both Eddas with unusual economy: the lifting of Hrungnir's leg, the gift of Gullfaxi, and the inheritance of the hammer after the end of the world.[^1]

### The Duel at Grjótúnagarðar (Skáldskaparmál 17)

The background is one of [[thor|Þórr]]'s greatest fights. The stone-hearted giant [[hrungnir|Hrungnir]] rode his gold-maned stallion Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr on the heels of [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s wager over whose horse was fastest; feasted, he drank and boasted he would carry off Valhǫll and kill every god but Freyja and [[sif|Sif]]. Þórr was summoned, and the duel was set at Grjótúnagarðar, the stone courts. The giants built Hrungnir a companion of clay, Mǫkkurkálfi, nine leagues tall and with a mare's heart that failed him; Hrungnir himself came with heart, shield, and weapon all of stone. Þjálfi tricked him into standing on his shield, and Þórr hurled Mjǫllnir through the raised whetstone — a shard lodged in Þórr's own head — and Hrungnir crashed forward, his leg across Þórr's neck.[^1]

### Three Nights Old (Skáldskaparmál 17)

Þjálfi could not lift the leg, and when all the Æsir had come, none of them could move it either. Then Magni arrived — the son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa, and he was three nights old — and he flung the leg off his father, saying it was a shame he had not come sooner: he thought he could have struck the giant dead with his bare fist. Þórr gave him Gullfaxi, the horse Hrungnir had ridden; Óðinn said Þórr did wrong to give so fine a horse to the son of a giantess and not to his own father. It is the whole of Magni's boyhood in one scene — and the only childhood the Edda gives any of the gods.[^1]

### The Hammer After (Vafþrúðnismál 51)

In the wisdom-contest, when Óðinn has wrung the fates of the gods from the giant Vafþrúðnir, one answer carries the brothers past the end of the world: 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done.' Vingnir is Þórr's own name. The prophecy does not flinch from what it costs — the father falls — and it states the inheritance plainly: the weapon passing whole into the hands of the sons.[^2]

### The Sons at Íðavöllr (Gylfaginning 51, 53)

At [[ragnarok|Ragnarǫk]] Þórr meets [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]], the Midgard serpent, and strikes it dead — and walks nine paces before he falls to its venom. But the world does not end there: in Snorri's vision of the green earth after the fire, the survivors gather at Íðavöllr — Baldr and Höðr return from Hel, reconciled, and 'Þórr's sons Móði and Magni shall come there, and they shall have Mjöllnir.' The hammer survives the god.[^3]

### The Father's Boast (Hárbarðsljóð 53)

The Poetic Edda's other notice of Magni is genealogical: trading insults with the disguised ferryman, Þórr names himself at full strength — 'I am Óðinn's son, Meili's brother, and Magni's father' (*Magna faðir*). Of all his titles, the name he closes with is his son's. Skáldskaparmál's kennings agree, styling Þórr 'father of Magni and [[modi|Móði]] and [[thrud|Þrúðr]]'.[^4]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17 (the Hrungnir duel; Magni, three nights old; the gift of Gullfaxi), trans. Faulkes (1987).
Vafþrúðnismál 51, trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 51 (Þórr and the serpent) and 53 (the renewed world), trans. Faulkes (1987).
Hárbarðsljóð 53, trans. Larrington (2014); Skáldskaparmál, kennings for Þórr, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Magni's scene belongs to one of the oldest hero-patterns in the Indo-European world: the prodigious infant. Greek tradition sets it at the beginning of [[herakles|Hēraklēs]]' life — the baby strangling the serpents in his cradle, told by Apollodorus and sung by Pindar in the first Nemean ode — and Irish tradition builds the boyhood deeds of [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] on the same armature, the *macgnímrada* of the Táin, where a child performs the feats of grown champions.[^1] The North compressed the whole pattern into a single sentence: three nights old, and already the strongest person in the story. The comparison is one of motif, not borrowing — Simek and Lindow treat Magni as a native figure of the Þórr-complex, and no line of transmission is needed.[^2]

His name, meanwhile, is ordinary Germanic vocabulary: *maginą, 'strength', an element that built personal names across the North — so the strongest boy in the Edda wears the plainest possible label. Within the corpus, his closest kin are [[modi|Móði]], the brother named beside him in both inheritance passages, and [[thor|Þórr]], the father whose deed he completes and whose weapon he carries out of the fire.[^2]

sources.citation: Apollodorus, The Library 2.4.8 (Herakles strangling the serpents), trans. J. G. Frazer, Loeb Classical Library (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1921); Pindar, Nemean 1; Táin Bó Cúailnge, macgnímrada (the boyhood deeds).

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Magni; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Magni, Móði.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Magni's afterlife ran quiet for centuries: the Icelandic given name *Magni* never died out, and Victorian mythographies kept the Hrungnir duel in circulation as one of Þórr's set-pieces — the Kearys' *The Heroes of Asgard* (1857) retold it for generations of children.[^1]

The twenty-first century put the brothers back on stage. Marvel Comics introduced Magni Thorson, a future son of Thor, in the 'Reigning' storyline of *Thor* in the early 2000s; and Santa Monica Studio's *God of War* (2018) cast Magni and Modi as their father's enforcers, carrying the pair to an audience far larger than the Edda's.[^2] Modern Heathenry keeps him among the sons of the Æsir honored for the survival of the world after Ragnarǫk — the generation for whom the hammer is kept.

sources.citation: Keary, Annie, and Eliza Keary, The Heroes of Asgard: Tales from Scandinavian Mythology (London: Macmillan, 1857).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Magni.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Magni is a purely textual figure: no runestone invokes him as a god, no votive deposit or place-name can be securely tied to his cult, and no picture stone has been convincingly read as the lifting of Hrungnir's leg.[^1] The material record keeps only his name's raw material: *Magni* occurs as an ordinary human personal name in Viking-Age runic inscriptions, built on the same *magn* 'strength' element that names the god.[^2]

The textual witnesses hang by the usual thin threads: *Vafþrúðnismál*, *Hárbarðsljóð*, and *Vǫluspá* in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); Skáldskaparmál in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister manuscripts; and the giantess þulur of the Skáldskaparmál, which list his mother Járnsaxa among the troll-women.[^1]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Magni, Hrungnir.
Peterson, Lena, Nordiskt runnamnslexikon, 5th ed. (Uppsala: Institutet för språk och folkminnen, 2007), s.v. Magni.

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic Edda knows Magni in three touches, and each one carries weight. *Vafþrúðnismál* 51 gives him the inheritance: asked what follows the end of the world, the giant answers that 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done' — Vingnir being Þórr's own name, so the prophecy names the hammer and the father's death in the same breath.[^1]

*Hárbarðsljóð* 53 supplies the genealogy from the father's side: closing his flyting with the disguised ferryman, Þórr names himself 'Óðinn's son, Meili's brother, and Magni's father' (*Magna faðir*) — of all his titles, the one he reaches for is his son's.[^2] And *Vǫluspá* 56 sets the cost of the inheritance: at Ragnarǫk Þórr strikes the Midgard serpent dead and walks nine paces from it, dying of its venom — the 'fighting done' that the prophecy of Vafþrúðnismál measured the inheritance against.[^3]

sources.citation: Vafþrúðnismál 51 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Hárbarðsljóð 53 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vǫluspá 56 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The Prose Edda is Magni's great witness. Skáldskaparmál 17 tells the whole of his boyhood inside the Hrungnir narrative: the giant's boast in Ásgarðr, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar with the whetstone and the clay companion, the fallen leg across Þórr's neck that no Æsir could move — and then Magni, son of Þórr and Járnsaxa, three nights old, flinging it off and wishing aloud that he had come sooner, for he could have felled the giant with his fist. The chapter closes with the gift of Gullfaxi and Óðinn's reproof: so fine a horse should not go to the son of a giantess.[^1]

Gylfaginning frames the same figure eschatologically: chapter 51 gives Þórr's death nine paces from the slain serpent, and chapter 53 gathers the survivors of Ragnarǫk at Íðavöllr, where 'Þórr's sons Móði and Magni shall come, and they shall have Mjöllnir.'[^2] The kennings for Þórr elsewhere in Skáldskaparmál keep the household in order — 'father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr' — and the giantess þulur preserve the name of Magni's mother Járnsaxa among the troll-women.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 51 and 53, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, kennings for Þórr and the giantess þulur, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The runic corpus contains no invocation of the god Magni. No runestone asks his favour and no inscription links a dedicant to his cult — a silence he shares with most of the younger generation of the Æsir, and one that marks him as a literary-mythological figure rather than a cult deity.[^1]

What the inscriptions do preserve is the name itself as ordinary Scandinavian anthroponymy: *Magni* occurs as a human personal name in the Viking-Age runic record, collected in Peterson's *Nordiskt runnamnslexikon*, and its first element *magn* 'strength' stands behind a whole family of Germanic strength-names. The theonym is thus the commonest kind of divine name in the North — a quality walked out of the name-pool and into mythology.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Magni.
Peterson, Lena, Nordiskt runnamnslexikon, 5th ed. (Uppsala: Institutet för språk och folkminnen, 2007), s.v. Magni.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond the Eddas, Magni's medieval afterlife is onomastic rather than narrative. Saxo Grammaticus, who euhemerizes much of the gods' dossier in the Gesta Danorum, gives no corresponding account of the Hrungnir duel and no role to a Magni — a reminder that Snorri's Skáldskaparmál is the tradition's principal and perhaps sole narrative home for the lifting of the leg.[^1]

As a human name, *Magni* lived on in Iceland and the wider North — it survives in the medieval record and remains a living Icelandic masculine name today, its meaning ('the strong one') never needing explanation.[^2] The contrast is instructive: the god has two scenes and a prophecy, but the name has an unbroken thousand-year history of ordinary bearers — the strongest name in the Edda worn by farmers, priests, and singers ever since.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Magni is the Edda's answer to the question every parent eventually asks: will anyone be strong enough when I cannot stand up? The myth answers it twice. Once at Grjótúnagarðar, where the whole company of the gods heaves at a dead giant's leg and fails, and a three-night-old boy walks up and does it — strength, the story insists, is not a function of age or rank, and help can arrive from the person everyone overlooked.[^1]

And once at the end of the world, where the father kills the serpent, walks nine paces, and falls — and the hammer is not buried with him. Móði and Magni carry Mjǫllnir into the green world. The Edda does not promise that the strong live forever. It promises that strength, like the hammer, is inheritable.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17 and Gylfaginning 51, 53, trans. Faulkes (1987).
